subject: system-design
title: Reliability
summary: The probability a system keeps doing the right thing over time, and why that's a different promise from merely being up.

blocks.text: Reliability is the probability that a system performs correctly over a period of time. It's not just about being reachable. It's about giving the right answer, every time, for as long as the work runs. A reliable system keeps its promises continuously, not just at the instant you check on it.

Availability asks 'is it up?'; reliability asks 'is it doing the right thing?'. The two come apart in both directions. A service can be fully available, answering every request, while returning corrupted or wrong data, so it's available but unreliable. Another can be rock-solid correct yet go down for a brief maintenance window: reliable but, in that moment, unavailable.

blocks.title: A crisp contrast
blocks.text: An API that responds instantly but charges the wrong amount is available and unreliable. A flawless service that's briefly offline for a deploy is reliable but unavailable. They measure different things.

Reliability comes from designing to keep working despite component faults. Redundancy and replication mean no single failure produces a wrong result; you also need validation, retries on idempotent operations, and checks that catch corruption before it reaches a user. The aim is correctness that survives the inevitable failure of individual parts.

items: Replicate data so one bad disk can't lose or corrupt the truth.
Validate inputs and outputs to catch wrong results, not just missing ones.
Make operations idempotent so a safe retry can't double-apply an effect.

blocks.text: Reliability tends to imply availability, since a system that keeps working correctly is usually also up. But the implication is one-directional and imperfect: being available says nothing about being correct, and you can be highly reliable yet still have planned moments of downtime. Don't read a strong uptime number as proof the answers are right.
So design for both, but separately: availability keeps the lights on, reliability keeps the answers true. A system needs to earn each one on its own.
